newsitem.title: UK: Intervention not seen as a major threat at present.
newsitem.headline: Intervention not seen as a major threat at present.

text.p: Foreign exchange traders are starting to talk about the chance of central bank action to rein in the soaring dollar, but most analysts see co-ordinated intervention unlikely around current levels.
The February Group of Seven (G7) meeting in Berlin raised fears of intervention with its statement, "We believe that major misalignments in exchange markets...have been corrected."

But these worries were soon forgotten as sound economic fundamentals pointed to a still higher dollar and as the market came to the conclusion that of G7, Japan was the only country to have major worries about the dollar's strength.
Since the meeting the dollar has risen a further 4.5 percent on the mark and 3.5 percent on the yen, but its progress has been orderly and soundly based.
"I think they are still quite happy to see it go," said Carlo Galazzi, forex manager at Nikko Bank in London.
"Obviously if it goes too far too quickly then they will try and stop it but it doesn't look like it's going to run away. The rise is quite orderly and I don't see much likelihood of intervention."

Although relatively relaxed at present, the market will start to get more jittery in the run-up to the Group of Seven get-together after the Washington IMF meeting at the end of the month. The week long IMF meeting starts on April 23 but the G7 finance ministers and central bankers hold talks on the 27th.

"The market is a bit suspicious that the central banks have been so quiet for so long and these recent comments, particularly from Japan, have raised some worries that they might be getting ready to smooth the dollar's rise a little," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
On Wednesday Japan's senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara said intervention is possible "...in cases in which rates deviate greatly from economic fundamentals."
The problem for the officials is that the dollar is not deviating from economic fundamentals given it yields 2.5 percent more than the mark and five percent more than the yen.
And those yield differentials will widen more as the U.S. raises rates further to fend of future inflation pressure while Japan and Germany keep rates low to help stimulate growth.

"If you are a central bank you've just got to wait for this rally to blow itself out," said one London based trader. "Intervention by Japan on it's own in its own time zone is quite likely at some stage but I don't think Germany or the U.S. would want any part in co-ordinated action at current levels."
"We are still looking to buy on dips and there is no real reason to cut back long positions substantially."
Eventually the dollar's rally will blow itself out as the Japanese trade surplus continues to bulge as the yen remains weak.
"The dollar's rally is sowing the seeds of its own demise as the Japanese surplus will continue to rise while the yen remains or gets weaker," CIBC Coleman said.
"Eventually the U.S. will just say, this is not on, but we are not at that stage yet because the dollar hasn't been going up for long enough...but it will come."
